title: C2PA provenance and deepfake detection — why fraud teams need both
summary: C2PA provenance records where media came from. Deepfake detection checks the media itself. Here's why fraud and claims teams need both.
body_markdown:
Provenance documents where a file says it came from. Detection checks the media itself. Fraud and claims teams that run both can answer both questions under legal scrutiny.


C2PA content provenance attaches a signed record to media showing which device or tool created it and how it was edited. Deepfake detection analyzes the audio, video, or image itself for signs of AI generation or manipulation. Provenance answers where content came from. Detection answers whether it's synthetic. Fraud teams need both answers.


Your fraud team finds a deepfake. Proving it in court is a different job. Investigators get asked which tool created the file, when it was made, and whether the version in front of them is the original or an edited copy. Detection identifies synthetic media. Provenance documents where media came from. They're different questions about the same problem, and the teams that can answer both are the ones whose evidence holds up.


## **What does C2PA content provenance prove?**


The[Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA)](https://c2pa.org/) publishes an open technical standard for attaching a cryptographically signed record to digital media. When a C2PA-compatible camera or app creates a file, it records the tool that made it, when it was made, and any later edits made in compatible software. That record is called content credentials, and it travels with the file as a verifiable chain of custody.


When a file carries intact credentials, a fraud investigator or claims adjuster can check its origin, creation tool, and edit history from capture to submission. That fits how investigators already think about evidence. A file with an unbroken, signed record is easier to defend in a legal or regulatory proceeding than one backed by a detection score alone. The examiner doesn't have to trust a model's output. They can check the signature.


What a signature proves is narrower than it sounds. It shows the record is intact and who signed it. It doesn't show that what the camera captured was real.


## **Where does C2PA provenance fall short?**


Three limits matter for any fraud team weighing provenance as a standalone control.


### **Honest credentials can describe a deepfake**


C2PA doesn't detect deepfakes. When a C2PA-compatible AI generator creates synthetic media, the file carries credentials that accurately say an AI tool made it. The origin is verifiable. The content is still synthetic. A face generated by a compliant tool has honest provenance, and it's still a deepfake.


### **Fraud content can arrive with no credentials**


Attackers can use generation tools that attach no credentials at all. Missing credentials don't prove a file is synthetic, because many legitimate cameras and apps don't support C2PA yet. Absence is still a risk signal, and it's where detection does its most important work.


### **Platforms strip credentials in transit**


Many platforms still strip metadata, including C2PA credentials, during upload and compression. A file signed at capture can reach a claims queue with its credentials gone. The C2PA specification now supports durable credentials, which pair the signed record with an invisible watermark or fingerprint so the record can be recovered after stripping. Adoption is still uneven, so stripping limits provenance as a standalone fraud signal.


Detection covers what provenance can't. It analyzes the media itself, so it works on files with missing credentials, tampered credentials, or honest credentials saying an AI tool made them. It doesn't need a chain of custody or any metadata at all.


## **How do provenance and deepfake detection work together?**


Each system covers the other's main weakness, which is why the strongest fraud controls run both.


Provenance on authentic content sets a baseline. When content your own teams create carries intact credentials, investigators can confirm its origin without relying on detection alone. Detection effort then goes to everything else. That means files with no credentials, broken credentials, or credentials that declare AI generation.


Detection catches what provenance can't see. That includes media from tools that attach nothing, files whose credentials were stripped in transit, and synthetic media presented next to records that look legitimate.


For fraud investigators and claims adjusters, the combination gives a fuller evidentiary picture. Content with intact credentials and a detection result that finds no manipulation carries more weight than either signal alone. Content with no credentials and a detection result that flags manipulation gives the reviewer both a flag and a forensic basis to escalate.


Regulation is pushing in the same direction.[The EU AI Act requires deepfakes to be disclosed and labeled, with obligations applying from August 2026.](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/50/) Provenance records are a natural place to carry that label. Detection matters for content that shows up without one, whether the tool didn't comply or someone removed the label on purpose.


The two signals also answer different questions in a dispute. Detection tells an investigator how likely it is that content is synthetic. Provenance tells them what a signed record says about where it came from. Detection alone flags synthetic media but can't always document the chain of custody for authentic files. Provenance alone verifies compliant files but can't flag synthetic media that arrives unsigned. Together they identify what's synthetic and document what's real.


## **How should enterprises roll out detection and provenance?**


Most enterprises deploy detection before provenance, and that order is right. Detection works on the media you already receive, whether or not it carries credentials. Provenance depends on adoption at the point of creation, through tools the enterprise often doesn't control. Starting with detection means you can identify synthetic media now instead of waiting for provenance coverage to catch up.


1.


**Deploy detection on inbound media first.** Reality Defender is detection-only, multimodal. RealScan analyzes uploaded audio, video, and image files, and RealAPI builds the same detection into your existing fraud and claims systems. Each file gets a verdict of Authentic, Suspicious, or Manipulated before human review begins.


2.


**Require provenance where you create content.** Mandate C2PA-compatible tools for internal media capture and production. That builds a provenance baseline investigators can check when they review content your own teams produced. This stage covers the workflows you control directly.


3.


**Route each file by what it carries.** Content your enterprise creates carries verifiable credentials. Content arriving from outside goes through detection. An investigator reviewing a claim gets a provenance record for files with a clear origin and a detection result for files without one. That closes the gap attackers use when they submit synthetic media into workflows that rely on human review alone.


Provenance tells you where a file says it came from. Detection tells you what's in it. Teams that need both answers should start with the one that works on every file they already receive.
